en.title: Largest Three-Digit Number Formed in Order
en.description:
Given an array of decimal digits, choose exactly three digits while keeping their relative order in the array, and concatenate them into a three-digit number; find the largest number that can be formed. The leading digit must be nonzero. The answer to the fixed upstream example [7,4,3,8,2] is 782; this matches choosing 7, 8, 2 in order, whereas rearranging the digits would give a different result.

Input ranges added by this site: 3≤N≤50, 0≤nums[i]≤9. This site uses standard input/output and does not claim that these constraints or this protocol come from the original OA.
The original OA does not define the return value when no valid three-digit number exists; this site explicitly specifies that -1 is output in that case.

Original source: https://oamaster.com/docs/companies/google#21-find-largest-number-google-early-career (content fingerprint of the fixed OAMaster snapshot: df9e04f772003ef1996bb410a0e9712db3d5fb1c857806257d19cdbea2362698). Material on the same problem: https://www.1point3acres.com/interview/problems/google-find-largest-number; that material only confirms choosing three elements from the array to form the largest three-digit number and provides no order-preserving example.
en.input: The first line contains an integer N; the second line contains N integers nums[i].
en.output: Output the largest three-digit number that can be formed by choosing three digits in the original array's relative order; if there is no valid choice with a nonzero leading digit, output -1 (defined by this site).
en.explanation: Enumerate all index triples i<j<k, skip the combinations with nums[i]=0, compute the three-digit number, and take the maximum. N≤50, so O(N³) is enough.
hints: The choice must keep the indices increasing.
Enumerate three indices; a combination whose leading digit is zero is not a three-digit number.
